Scenario ID: SCN-007
Title: Archive — put a bookmark away without losing it
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour

Archiving a bookmark hides it from the Collection and from ordinary searches
(Collection and Reading list). It is not deleted: it lives in the Archive view,
where it can be found by searching within the Archive, and it can be restored to
the Collection at any time. Archiving and reading-list membership are independent
concepts serving different purposes.

## Gherkin

Feature: Archive

  Scenario: Archive hides a bookmark from the collection and ordinary search
    Given an active bookmark
    When I archive it
    Then it no longer appears in the Collection or Reading list
    And an ordinary search does not surface it

  Scenario: Archived bookmarks are kept and findable in the Archive
    Given an archived bookmark
    When I open the Archive view
    Then the bookmark is listed there
    And searching within the Archive can find it

  Scenario: Restore an archived bookmark
    Given an archived bookmark
    When I choose "Restore to collection"
    Then it returns to the Collection
    And its reading-list membership is unchanged

## Assumptions
- Restoring returns the bookmark to whatever reading-list state it had before
  archiving.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-006 (reading list), SCN-008 (views and search scope)

input.content:
Scenario ID: SCN-008
Title: Three views (Collection, Reading list, Archive) with search scoped to the current view
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour

The bookmarks are presented through three views selected by a control at the top:

- Collection: all active (non-archived) bookmarks, read or unread, whether or not
  they are on the reading list. New saves land here.
- Reading list: only active bookmarks the client has marked to read later.
- Archive: only bookmarks the client has explicitly archived.

Search is scoped to the current view: from the Collection or Reading list it
searches only active bookmarks and never surfaces archived ones; from the Archive
it searches only archived bookmarks. The match count names the scope (e.g. "in
your collection", "in the archive").

## Gherkin

Feature: Views and search scope

  Scenario: New saves appear only in the Collection
    When I save a new bookmark
    Then it appears in the Collection view
    And not in the Reading list unless I chose to read it later

  Scenario: Search is scoped to the current view
    Given both active and archived bookmarks
    When I search from the Collection or Reading list
    Then only active bookmarks can match, never archived ones
    And when I search from the Archive
    Then only archived bookmarks can match

## Assumptions
- The three views are mutually consistent projections of the same bookmarks by
  their archived / reading-list state.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-005 (search), SCN-006 (reading list), SCN-007 (archive)

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [SbE reaction loop]
- Approved scenarios: [5]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

content.text:
Please open the sample-loaded version at **http://maker:4001/?demo=edge** (I've also saved reference images at `prototypes/edge-collection.png`, `prototypes/edge-reading.png`, and `prototypes/edge-archive.png`).

Have a look, and tell me if any of these edge situations feel wrong:

1. **The very first card** — a punishingly long title, a long note, seven tags, and a long web address. Does it still read calmly, or does it feel cramped/broken to you?
2. **The second card** is a **bare** bookmark — just a title and link, no note or tags. Is that clean minimum fine, or would you want it nudging you to add something?
3. **The bottom card** has a giant single-word address and tag — confirm nothing spills off the side.
4. **Try a bad input:** in the top box type something that isn't a link (like `just some words`) and press Add — it should gently decline and not save anything.
5. You'll notice several **letter badges** instead of site icons — that's the graceful fallback when an icon can't be loaded. Fine as-is?

And two genuine questions I can't answer for you:

- **Deleting for good.** Right now nothing is ever truly deleted — "putting away" means Archive, which you can always restore. Is that what you want, or do you also need a way to **permanently delete** a bookmark you're sure you'll never want again?
- **Seeing when you saved something.** Cards don't currently show a date. When you're looking back through a long collection, would a small **"saved on…" date** help you trust and place things — or is it unnecessary?

Once we've settled these, I'll have covered the corners and can propose building the real thing.

content:
The edge examples hold together well. The long title, note, tags, and address wrap without breaking the card, and the unusually long tag and address stay within the layout. The bare bookmark is fine as a clean minimum; I don’t need repeated prompts to add notes or tags. The invalid-link response and letter-badge fallback also feel appropriate.

I do need permanent deletion as a separate action from Archive. Archive should remain reversible, while Delete should clearly warn me that the bookmark will be removed for good and ask for confirmation.

A small saved date would be useful, especially in a large collection. Keep it quiet, but show when the bookmark was added; retaining when it was last updated would also help when editing older items.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [8]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

base = pathlib.Path("prototypes/index.html").resolve().as_uri()
errs=[]
def titles(pg): return [t.inner_text() for t in pg.query_selector_all('.item .title')]
def find(pg,title):
    for el in pg.query_selector_all('.item'):
        if el.query_selector('.title').inner_text().startswith(title): return el
def clickact(el,label):
    for bb in el.query_selector_all('.act'):
        if bb.inner_text()==label: bb.click(); return True
    return False
with sync_playwright() as p:
    b=p.chromium.launch(); pg=b.new_page()
    pg.on("console", lambda m: errs.append(m.text) if m.type=="error" and "esource" not in m.text else None)
    pg.on("pageerror", lambda e: errs.append("PAGEERROR: "+str(e)))
    pg.goto(base+"?demo=edge"); pg.wait_for_selector('[data-harness-ready="true"]'); pg.wait_for_selector('.item')
    # dates
    print("k1 dates:", find(pg,'The remarkably').query_selector('.card-dates').inner_text())
    print("carbonara dates:", find(pg,'Proper carbonara').query_selector('.card-dates').inner_text())
    n0=len(pg.query_selector_all('.item'))
    # delete flow with cancel then confirm
    el=find(pg,'Async guide')
    clickact(el,'Delete')
    warn=el.query_selector('.confirm-text').inner_text()
    print("confirm warning:",warn)
    clickact(el,'Cancel')
    print("after cancel count same:", len(pg.query_selector_all('.item'))==n0)
    el=find(pg,'Async guide')
    clickact(el,'Delete')
    clickact(find(pg,'Async guide'),'Delete permanently')
    print("async guide gone:", find(pg,'Async guide') is None, "| count:", len(pg.query_selector_all('.item')))
    # edit bumps updated -> shows Updated today
    el=find(pg,'Proper carbonara'); clickact(el,'Edit'); pg.wait_for_selector('.review')
    pg.fill('#fDesc','Dinner idea (updated)'); pg.click('#doSave')
    print("carbonara dates after edit:", find(pg,'Proper carbonara').query_selector('.card-dates').inner_text())
    b.close()
print("ERRORS:",errs)

Both are in and verified. Please confirm at **http://maker:4001/?demo=edge**:

1. **Quiet dates:** each card now shows a small **"Saved …"** date at the bottom. The very first card also shows **"· Updated …"** because it was changed later; cards saved and untouched show only the saved date. Does that quiet treatment feel right — present but not shouting?
2. **Permanent delete:** on any card press **Delete**. It doesn't delete immediately — it asks **"Delete for good? This can't be undone."** with a red **Delete permanently** and a **Cancel**. Try **Cancel** (nothing happens), then **Delete** → **Delete permanently** on something you don't mind losing, and confirm it's gone. Note this is entirely separate from **Archive**, which stays reversible.

Two choices I'd like you to confirm:

- **The "Updated" date only appears when a bookmark was changed on a later day** than it was saved — so a quick fix right after saving won't clutter it with a redundant "updated today." Is showing it only on genuinely-later edits what you'd want?
- **Delete sits on every card** (Collection, Reading list, and Archive alike), not only in the Archive. Does having it always available suit you, or would you rather permanent deletion live only in the Archive, as the final step after putting something away?

Once you're happy with these, I believe we've covered the corners — and I'll summarise everything that's settled and ask whether to start building the real thing.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an

content.text:
That covers the corners. Here's everything we've settled together — your one calm place for links:

**Saving**
- Paste a link and it gathers the page's title, a description, its icon, and a preview image for you; you can correct the title and description before saving, and edit them anytime after.
- Saving the same link twice never makes a duplicate — it takes you to the one you already have so you can update it.
- Something that isn't a link is gently declined; nothing is saved by mistake.

**Organising & finding** — the heart of it
- Your own tags, with fast reuse (type to narrow your existing tags, or create a new one) so you don't end up with near-duplicates.
- Search across everything you remember — title, your notes, tags, site name, and the full address — with refinements when you want them (`#tag`, "exact phrases", and `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` with brackets). A calm "no matches" message when nothing fits, and it never breaks on a malformed search.

**Three spaces, kept separate**
- **Collection:** all your active bookmarks.
- **Reading list:** only what you deliberately mark to read later (at save time or after); "mark as read" clears it from the list but keeps it in your collection.
- **Archive:** things you've put away — hidden from the collection and ordinary searches, but never lost and always restorable. Search stays within whichever space you're in.

**Trust & housekeeping**
- Quiet "saved" (and, for later edits, "updated") dates on each card.
- Permanent **Delete**, separate from Archive, always behind a clear "this can't be undone" confirmation.
- A calm layout that holds up with long titles, lots of tags, and bare entries — and sensible empty states everywhere.

I've noted a few **non-functional** wishes for later (comfortable on the phone, staying snappy with hundreds of bookmarks, the overall "calm" feel).

That's **12 settled behaviours**, and I think it fully covers the goal you set out: *always being able to find and trust what you saved.*

**May I now switch from exploring to actually building this as the real application?** Nothing new to try in this message — just your go-ahead (or tell me anything that still feels unfinished).

I’m not ready to start building yet—the summary captures what we explored, but a few important parts of the application remain unfinished.

I still want to work through:

- Editing the address, tags, and a personal note—not just the title and description. The note should be separate from the page’s description, support simple formatting, and display properly when I view it.
- Clicking a bookmark to open the original page, and clicking a tag to filter the collection by that tag.
- Sorting by things such as date added or title.
- Selecting several bookmarks—or all bookmarks in the current search or view—and then adding or removing tags, marking them read or unread, archiving them, or deleting them together.
- Saving a useful search and its included or excluded tags for reuse.
- Keeping a saved copy of the page in case the original disappears. For a PDF, I’d want the PDF kept instead; saving to the Internet Archive would also be useful.
- Importing my existing browser bookmarks and exporting them again without losing their titles, tags, or original saved dates.
- A few personal display choices, such as my default sorting, how many items are shown, and text size.

Those are closely connected to organising, finding, and trusting what I save, so I’d like us to explore them before implementation begins.

Scenario ID: SCN-001
Title: Save a new link with reviewed details
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour

The client pastes a link's address into a single "Add" field and chooses Add.
The app gathers the page's information automatically — its real title, a short
description, the site's small icon, and the page's preview image when one is
available — and presents a review panel pre-filled with them. The title and
description are editable, so the client can simply confirm them or correct them
before saving. On Save, the bookmark is added to the top of the list (newest
first). The saved card shows, from top to bottom: the preview image (when the
page has one), the title, the client's description, the link address, and a
quiet source line carrying the site icon and site name — styled as source
context, clearly distinct from the client's own tags rather than as a tag pill.

When a page has no preview image, the card is shown without an image area at all;
no placeholder box is used, keeping the layout calm.

The overall experience is a calm, uncluttered single column.

## Gherkin

Feature: Saving a link

  Scenario: Save a new link with reviewed details
    Given the bookmark list (which may be empty)
    When I enter a link's address and choose Add
    Then the app gathers the page's title, description, site icon, and preview
         image when one is available
    And a review panel is shown pre-filled with those details
    And the title and description are editable
    When I optionally correct the title or description and choose Save
    Then the bookmark is added to the top of the list, newest first
    And its card shows the preview image when available, the title, my
        description, the link, and a quiet source line with the site icon and name

  Scenario: Save a page that has no preview image
    Given a page that has no preview image available
    When I save it
    Then its card is shown without any image area
    And no placeholder image box is displayed

## Assumptions

- Auto-collected details (title, description, icon, preview image) are read from
  the target page in the real application; the Phase 1 prototype simulates the
  title/icon/preview to demonstrate the flow, not the fetch accuracy.
- The description field currently doubles as the client's own editable note; the
  distinction between the page's description and a separate personal note is not
  yet explored (candidate for a later exploration step).
- Newest-first ordering.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [12]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [13]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [13]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [15]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

Scenario ID: SCN-016
Title: Select multiple bookmarks and act on them together
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour

Each card has a selection checkbox. When one or more bookmarks are selected, an
action bar appears showing the number selected, a "Select all" that selects every
bookmark matching the current view and search (the whole match set, not merely the
cards on screen — the bar names the true total, e.g. "Select all 137 matching
bookmarks"), and "Clear".

From the action bar the client can, on all selected bookmarks at once:
- Add a tag or remove a tag (via one tag field; selection is kept after applying,
  so several changes can be made in sequence).
- Mark as read or Mark as unread.
- Archive them (or, in the Archive view, Restore them to the collection).
- Delete them, behind the same clear "this can't be undone" confirmation as a
  single delete.

In the Archive view the read/unread and Archive actions are replaced by Restore,
since archived bookmarks are not on the reading list. Selection is scoped to the
current view and search: items that leave the current view as a result of an
action drop out of the selection automatically.

## Gherkin

Feature: Bulk actions

  Scenario: Select all matching bookmarks
    Given a view and/or search with several matching bookmarks
    When I choose "Select all"
    Then every bookmark matching the current view and search is selected
    And the action bar states the total number matching

  Scenario: Add or remove a tag across the selection
    Given several bookmarks are selected
    When I add a tag to the selection
    Then that tag is applied to all of them and they remain selected
    And when I remove a tag from the selection
    Then that tag is removed from all of them

  Scenario: Mark read / unread in bulk
    Given several selected bookmarks
    When I choose Mark as read or Mark as unread
    Then all of them leave or join the reading list accordingly

  Scenario: Archive / restore / delete in bulk
    Given several selected bookmarks
    When I choose Archive (or Restore in the Archive view)
    Then all of them are archived (or restored)
    And when I choose Delete and confirm
    Then all of them are permanently removed after one confirmation

## Assumptions
- "Select all" always spans the full matching set across any future paging or
  display limit, not just the currently rendered cards.
- Selection persists across tag add/remove; it prunes to what remains visible
  after other actions.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-004 (tags), SCN-006 (reading list), SCN-007 (archive), SCN-009 (delete)

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [15]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [16]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

Scenario ID: SCN-017
Title: Save a search (with its included/excluded tags and view) for reuse
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour

The client can save the current search for reuse. A saved search captures exactly
what is in the search box — words, phrases, included tags (#tag) and excluded tags
(NOT #tag) — together with the view it was made in (Collection, Reading list, or
Archive). The client names it; the default name is the query text.

Saved searches appear as named chips beneath the search box. Clicking a chip
re-applies that search and returns to the view it was saved in (a search saved in
the Archive reopens in the Archive; one saved in the Reading list reopens there).
The × on a chip removes it. Applying a saved search does not change the current
sort order.

## Gherkin

Feature: Saved searches

  Scenario: Save the current search
    Given an active search (which may include or exclude tags)
    When I choose Save and give it a name
    Then it is stored as a named saved search shown beneath the search box

  Scenario: Apply a saved search restores query and view
    Given a saved search made in a particular view
    When I click its chip
    Then its exact query is applied
    And I am returned to the view it was saved in
    And the current sort order is unchanged

  Scenario: Remove a saved search
    When I click the × on a saved-search chip
    Then that saved search is removed

## Assumptions
- A saved search stores query + view, not sort order (sort stays as the client's
  current/preferred order).

## Related scenarios
- SCN-005 (search), SCN-008 (views), SCN-015 (sorting)
